title: Contracts, ownership and accounts
summary: Who owns the code, the domain, the hosting accounts and the API keys, and how to set things up so the client owns everything and you hold a key.
youWillLearn: The few clauses every small client contract needs
Why code does not automatically belong to the client who paid, and how IP assignment fixes it
Why the client should own every account, domain and API key from day one
How to move a project you started in your own accounts

glossary.code repo: Short for repository: the folder of an app's code and its full history, stored online on a site like GitHub.
glossary.statement of work: The part of a contract that describes exactly what will be delivered. Often it points to the signed scope doc.
glossary.IP: Intellectual property: legal ownership of creative work such as code, designs and text.
glossary.IP assignment: A contract clause that moves ownership of the work from the person who made it to the client, usually once paid in full.
glossary.pre-existing IP: Tools, templates or code you made before this project and reuse across clients. You keep it and grant the client a license to use it.
glossary.warranty: A promise to fix defects in your own work for free, for a set period after launch.
glossary.registrar: The company where a domain name is registered and renewed, and whose account controls it.
glossary.DNS: The internet's address book: records that point a domain name to the servers that host the site.
glossary.environment variable: A named setting given to the app when it runs, like an API key, kept outside the code.
glossary.transfer: Moving a repo, project or database from one account or organization to another without rebuilding it.

steps.title: Sam's app runs on four accounts
body: Sam owns a small hair salon; you are building her booking app. It rests on four things: the code repo (the stored code), hosting (servers that run it and its data), the domain (the salon's web address) and an AI key (a password for Claude, the AI).
To move fast, you set all four up in your own accounts.

scene.caption: Code, hosting, domain and AI key: all four sit in your accounts.

steps.title: A year later: whose app is it?
body: A year after launch, Sam wants another developer to add a feature. Then it turns out: the code, the hosting, the domain and the AI key are all in your accounts, some on your card.
Sam paid for an app she cannot move without you. Nobody planned it, but it works like a hostage situation.
changes: + Arrow from Sam to You: she has to ask
~ Sam: paid for the app, but cannot move it
~ Owned by Sam 0 of 4 is now a real problem

scene.caption: Everything Sam paid for sits inside your accounts.

steps.title: The client owns, you get a key
body: The rule: the client owns every account, and you are invited in as a member. Her business email, her card, her name on the domain.
You work the same way, with Claude Code and the dashboards. The difference shows on bad days: if you get sick, fall out, or Sam hires someone else, nothing has to be rescued.

callout.text: A builder renovating a house. The owner keeps the deed and hands the builder a key. When the job ends, the key comes back. Nobody puts the deed in the builder's name to save time.

changes: ~ Your accounts → Sam's accounts
~ You: an invited member
~ Owned by Sam 0 of 4 → 4 of 4
− Sam's "please?" arrow: she no longer has to ask

scene.caption: Same four accounts, new owner. Sam holds the deed; you hold a member key.

steps.title: The contract in six clauses
body: A small project contract covers six things: the statement of work (your scope doc), fees and milestones (your estimate), how changes work, who owns the result, a short warranty, and who owns the accounts.
Start from a lawyer-reviewed template for your country. This lesson tells you what to look for; it is not legal advice.

code.code:
1. Scope       the signed scope doc, v1.2
2. Fees        fixed fee, 3 milestones (30/40/30)
3. Changes     written change requests, quoted first
4. Ownership   assigned to client on full payment
5. Warranty    own bugs fixed free for 30 days
6. Accounts    client owns all accounts and keys
code.caption: One line per clause is enough to check a template covers what matters.

callout.text: Also look for a cap on your liability, confidentiality, and who is responsible for personal data. Bookings hold clients' names and phone numbers, so privacy law may apply to you both.

changes: − You, Hosting, Code Repo, AI Key, Domain: paper first
+ Scope Doc and Estimate: the plan and price you agreed
+ Contract: ties them together, signed by both

scene.caption: The contract ties together the scope, the price and the ownership rules.

steps.title: Who owns the code you write
body: In many countries, whoever writes code owns its copyright, even when someone else paid. So the contract needs an IP assignment: ownership of the custom work moves to Sam on full payment.
Two things stay outside it: your pre-existing IP, like a starter kit you reuse, and open-source packages (free code others publish), which keep their own licenses.

callout.text: Tie the assignment to final payment. It is fair to both sides: Sam gets full ownership the moment she has paid, and you keep leverage until then without holding her accounts hostage.

changes: − Scope Doc, Estimate, Contract, Sam: zoom into the code
+ Booking Flow, Database Design: custom, assigned to Sam
+ Starter Kit, Open Source: used, but only licensed

scene.caption: Custom work moves to Sam. Your toolkit and open source are only licensed.

steps.title: Sam signs up, you get invited
body: At kickoff, Sam creates each account with her business email and card: GitHub for the code repo, Vercel and Supabase for hosting (the app and its database), the AI provider for the key, a registrar for the domain. Then she invites you.
It takes one screen-share call. Bills land with her from day one (the pass-through from lesson 2).

callout.text: Do not run a client's business on your free personal plans. Vercel's Hobby plan, for example, is meant for personal, non-commercial use. Check each provider's terms and put commercial work on a team or paid plan in the client's name.

changes: − Booking Flow, Database Design, Starter Kit, Open Source
+ Sam, You and the four accounts, now in Sam's name
+ Code Repo, Hosting, AI Key, Domain: Sam creates each one
+ Invite: from Hosting to You

scene.caption: Sam creates each account. Invites flow out to you.

steps.title: The domain: never hold it yourself
body: Register the domain in Sam's name, in her own account at a registrar (the company that rents out domain names), with her email for renewals.
You only need access to its DNS, the records that point the domain at the hosting. If it sits in your account and a renewal slips, her business vanishes from the web.

code.filename: DNS records (values come from Vercel's domain settings)
code.code:
Type    Name   Value
A       @      the IP address Vercel shows you
CNAME   www    the target Vercel shows you
code.caption: Two records connect the domain to the hosting. Changing them is all you need access for.

callout.text: Turn on auto-renew and the transfer lock, and give a second person on Sam's side access to the registrar. Lapsed domains get registered by someone else and resold.

changes: + Sam → Domain: the domain is in her name
~ Domain: auto-renew on
~ You: may edit only its DNS records
− Invite arrow; Code Repo and AI Key fade back

scene.caption: Sam owns the domain. You only edit the records that point it at the hosting.

steps.title: API keys live in env vars, never in code
body: Each key belongs to the account that pays for it: Sam's AI key, Sam's SMS key. Make separate keys for development and the live app.
Keys go into environment variables (env vars) in the hosting settings, never into the code repo. Commit a .env.example with names only, so the next developer knows what to ask for.

code.code:
# Safe to commit: names only, never values
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL=
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=

# Server only: never add NEXT_PUBLIC_ to these
SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY=
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
SMS_API_KEY=
AI_MODEL=
code.caption: NEXT_PUBLIC_ values ship to the browser, so the publishable key is only safe with row-level security on. Older projects call these keys anon and service_role.

callout.text: Ask Claude Code: "List every env var the app reads." No secret may start with NEXT_PUBLIC_: that prefix ships the value to every visitor's browser. Check .env* is in .gitignore (files Git never saves). A key ever committed? Rotate it: new key, old one deleted.

changes: + AI Key → Hosting: stored there as an env var
~ Code Repo: holds no secrets
~ Domain fades back, AI Key comes forward
~ You: DNS only → member

scene.caption: The key is Sam's. It lives in the hosting's env vars, not in the code repo.

steps.title: Started in your account? Move it early
body: Sometimes you prototype in your own accounts before the contract is signed. That is fine if you move everything before launch, while it is small.
GitHub, Vercel and Supabase all let you transfer a project to another account. Put it in the estimate as a task. After launch, a move touches live data and keys, and gets risky.

callout.text: After a transfer, rotate the keys you created or saw: the AI key, the SMS key, the database secrets. A project should not leave your hands while you still hold working credentials to it.

changes: − Sam, You, AI Key, Domain
+ Your prototype: a Code Repo, Hosting and Database in your name
+ Database: the salon's data, moving across to Sam too
~ Code Repo and Hosting slide into Sam's accounts on the right

scene.caption: Each piece moves from your prototype accounts into Sam's, before launch.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A short contract covers scope, fees, changes, ownership, warranty and accounts. Custom code is assigned to the client on payment; your toolkit is licensed.
Sam owns every account, the domain and every key, on her email and card. You are a member. If you started in your accounts, transfer before launch and rotate the keys.
changes: ~ Your prototype copies fade out: everything lives with Sam

scene.caption: Everything lives in Sam's accounts. Your old copies are switched off.

quiz.question: Your contract says nothing about IP. Sam has paid in full. Who owns the code?

options.text: Sam, because she paid for it.
options.why: Paying does not automatically move copyright in many countries. Without an assignment clause, ownership can stay with the author.

options.text: It may well still be you, which is why the contract needs an IP assignment.
options.why: In many places the author holds copyright by default. An explicit assignment on full payment removes the doubt for both sides.

options.text: Nobody, because Claude Code wrote much of it.
options.why: How copyright treats AI-generated code is still unsettled, and your own choices and edits still count. The contract should state what Sam receives, whatever tools you used.

quiz.question: Sam wants to launch fast. What is the best way to set up hosting and the AI key?

options.text: Use your hosting account and your AI key, and bill her monthly.
options.why: It works until something changes. Then Sam cannot move without you, and you are paying her bills and carrying her usage risk.

options.text: Share your own login details with Sam so she has access too.
options.why: Shared logins break two-factor login and auditing, and the accounts are still yours. Ownership has not moved.

options.text: Sam creates the accounts on her card and invites you as a member.
options.why: She owns the assets and pays the providers directly. You get exactly the access you need, and it can be removed cleanly later.

quiz.question: Claude Code put NEXT_PUBLIC_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the env file so the browser can call the Claude API directly. What do you change?

options.text: Nothing, env vars are always secret.
options.why: Not with this prefix. Next.js bundles NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables into the browser code, where anyone can read them.

options.text: Drop the prefix and let the app server call the Claude API.
options.why: The key stays on the server. The browser asks your app server, which can check the user, limit their calls and then call the Claude API.

options.text: Keep it, but rotate the key every month.
options.why: A key visible in the browser can be copied within minutes of launch. Rotating monthly still leaves it exposed.

takeaways: Every client contract needs scope, fees, changes, ownership, warranty and account terms. Start from a lawyer-reviewed template.
Use an IP assignment on full payment for custom work, and license your reusable toolkit.
The client creates and pays for every account, the domain and every API key. You are invited as a member.
Secrets live in env vars, never in the repo and never with a NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix.
Prototyped in your own accounts? Transfer before launch, then rotate the keys.
